a: In the days when the judges ruled
p: The story is set in the time of the book of Judges, an age of chaos with no king.
b: The judges were local war leaders between Joshua and the first kings, roughly 1200 to 1050 BC. The book of Judges ends in civil war, kidnapping and gang rape, with the refrain "There was no king in Israel in those days. Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). Two of its worst stories start with a man from Bethlehem (Judges 17:7; 19:1). Ruth opens in that same world and in that same town, then shows ordinary people acting with kindness and ends with the birth of a king's family line (4:17).

a: there was a famine in the land
t: A famine sends a family away
p: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob's sons all left the promised land because of famine.
b: Famine drove Abraham to Egypt (Genesis 12:10), Isaac to the Philistines (Genesis 26:1), and Jacob's family to Egypt (Genesis 42–46). Later, Elisha told a woman to leave Israel for seven years during a famine (2 Kings 8:1–2). The Law warned that famine could be a sign of covenant trouble (Leviticus 26:19–20; Deuteronomy 28:23–24), but the narrator never says why this one came.

a: live as a foreigner
p: The verb means to live somewhere without the rights of a native. Ruth will later be one in Israel.
b: The Hebrew verb gur means to live as a ger, a resident foreigner: someone who settles in a land but has no family land and no full rights there. Abraham was a ger in Canaan (Genesis 23:4), and Israel was one in Egypt (Exodus 22:21). Elimelech's family plans a temporary stay. The roles then flip: the Israelites become the foreigners in Moab, and later the Moabite becomes the foreigner in Bethlehem (2:10). The Law commanded Israel to love the foreigner (Deuteronomy 10:18–19).

a: the fields of Moab
p: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Israel's stories about Moab were mostly bitter.
b: Moab was a kingdom on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, about 50 miles from Bethlehem. Genesis traces the Moabites to Lot and his older daughter (Genesis 19:30–38). Moab's king hired Balaam to curse Israel, and Moabite women led Israelites into idol worship (Numbers 22–25). The Law barred Moabites from the LORD's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3–6), and in Judges a Moabite king ruled Israel for 18 years (Judges 3:12–30). The Hebrew says "fields of Moab," a phrase repeated seven times in the book, which sets up a contrast with the field of Boaz in chapter 2.

a: Elimelech
p: "My God is king," in a time with no king. The sons' names may sound like "sickness" and "ending."
b: Elimelech means "my God is king," a pointed name in the days when "Israel had no king" (Judges 21:25). Naomi means "pleasant" or "my sweetness," which she will reject (1:20). Mahlon and Chilion sound like Hebrew words for "sickness" and "finishing" or "failing," and many readers have heard them as names chosen for the plot. Scholars disagree: some think they are real old names that happen to sound this way, others that the storyteller chose them to fit the plot (Campbell; Sasson).

a: Ephrathites
p: An old name tied to Bethlehem, used again for David's father and in Micah's prophecy.
b: Ephrathah is an old name for Bethlehem or for the clan that lived there. Rachel was buried "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (Genesis 35:19). David is introduced as "the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah whose name was Jesse" (1 Samuel 17:12). Micah later promised a ruler from "Bethlehem Ephrathah" (Micah 5:2), which Matthew applies to Jesus (Matthew 2:6). So the word quietly signals David's family from the first verses.

a: They married Moabite women
p: The Law banned marriage with Canaanites but not Moabites by name. Readers have long disagreed.
b: Deuteronomy 7:1–3 forbids marriage with seven Canaanite nations; Moab is not on the list. Deuteronomy 23:3 bars a Moabite from "the assembly of the LORD," and centuries later Ezra and Nehemiah broke up marriages with Moabite and other foreign wives (Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:1–3, 23–27). The Targum, the ancient Aramaic paraphrase, says the sons broke the law and died for it. The Mishnah instead ruled that the ban covers Moabite men but not women (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3), which made Ruth's later marriage lawful; the Talmud sums it up as "a Moabite, not a Moabitess" (Yevamot 76b). The book itself passes no judgment.
r: Deuteronomy 7:1–3; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Nehemiah 13:23–27; 1 Kings 11:1–2

a: her two boys
t: From two boys to one boy
p: Naomi loses her "boys" here and holds a "boy" again at the end. The same rare word frames the book.
b: The usual word for sons is banim, used in 1:1–3. Here the narrator switches to yeladim, "boys" or "children," a tender word used only here and in 4:16, where Naomi takes "the child" (hayyeled) into her lap. Many commentators see this as a deliberate frame: the book begins with a woman who has lost her boys and ends with a boy given back to her.

a: the LORD
p: When you see LORD in small capitals, the Hebrew has God's personal name, YHWH.
b: The Hebrew here is God's own name, written with four letters, YHWH. Out of reverence, Jewish readers stopped saying it aloud before the time of Jesus and said Adonai, "Lord," instead. Most English Bibles follow that custom and print "the LORD" in capitals; "the Lord" in lower case stands for Adonai. The pronunciation "Yahweh" is a scholarly reconstruction; "Jehovah" mixes the four letters with the vowels of Adonai. The name appears 18 times in Ruth, almost always in the characters' blessings and prayers.

a: had come to help his people
p: The KJV's "visited" means God stepped in, the same verb used for his rescue of Israel in Egypt.
b: The verb paqad (KJV "visited") means to pay attention to, take care of, or step in to act. God "visited" Sarah and she conceived (Genesis 21:1). Joseph promised that God would "visit" Israel and bring them out of Egypt (Genesis 50:24), and when Moses came, the people heard that the LORD had "visited" them (Exodus 4:31). Here the help is simple: bread.

a: bread
t: Bread returns to the House of Bread
p: Lechem, "bread," is the second half of Bethlehem's name. The famine is over.
b: Bethlehem means "house of bread" (beit lechem). Hebrew lechem can mean food in general, so many versions say "food," but the wordplay is plain to a Hebrew ear: the house of bread had no bread (1:1), and now it has bread again. Bread and grain run all through the book, from barley harvest (1:22) to the meal in the field (2:14) to the grain in Ruth's shawl (3:15). Christians later noticed that Jesus, "the bread of life" (John 6:35), was born in Bethlehem.

a: her mother's house
p: Normally a widow returned to her father's house. The "mother's house" shows up in love and marriage settings.
b: When a young widow went back to her family, the Bible usually speaks of her "father's house" (Genesis 38:11; Leviticus 22:13). "Mother's house" is rare. Rebekah ran to tell her "mother's household" about a marriage offer (Genesis 24:28), and the woman in the Song of Songs speaks of bringing her beloved to her mother's house (Song of Songs 3:4; 8:2). So Naomi may mean the place where marriages were arranged, which fits her wish that they find new husbands (1:9).
r: Genesis 24:28; Genesis 38:11; Song of Songs 3:4; Song of Songs 8:2

a: faithful love
p: The key word of the book. It means loyal love that goes beyond what duty requires.
b: Hesed has no single English equal. The KJV says "kindness" or "mercy"; others say "steadfast love," "loyalty" or "loving devotion." It is love shown inside a relationship, love that keeps faith when it would be easy not to, and it often goes beyond what anyone could demand. It is the word God uses of himself in Exodus 34:6–7. In Ruth it appears three times: Naomi prays for God's hesed on her daughters-in-law (1:8), she praises it in Boaz (2:20), and Boaz praises it in Ruth (3:10). A later rabbi said the book was written "to teach how great is the reward of those who do hesed" (Ruth Rabbah 2:14).

a: rest
p: Menuchah means security and a settled home. Naomi will come back to this word in 3:1.
b: Menuchah is the rest of a place where you belong and are safe. God promised Israel "rest" in the land (Deuteronomy 12:9; Joshua 21:44), and the psalmist is led "beside still waters," literally "waters of rest" (Psalm 23:2). For a widow in that world, a husband's house meant food, protection and standing. Naomi wishes this for her daughters-in-law here, and in 3:1 she sets out to find "a place of rest" for Ruth (3:1).

a: we will go back with you
t: Going "back" where they had never been
p: Shuv, "return," appears 12 times in chapter 1. Ruth "returns" to a land she has never seen.
b: The verb shuv, "turn back, return," is the key word of chapter 1: about twelve times in 22 verses. Naomi returns; she urges her daughters-in-law to return home; Orpah returns to her people and her gods; and Ruth, oddly, is said to "return" from Moab (1:22) to a land she has never seen. The same verb is Israel's word for repentance, turning back to God. The book closes the theme in 4:15, where the child will be one who "brings back" Naomi's life.

a: Are there still sons inside me
p: Naomi is thinking of the custom that a dead man's brother should marry his widow.
b: Israel's law said that if a man died with no son, his brother should marry the widow, and their first son would carry on the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). This is called levirate marriage, from the Latin levir, "brother-in-law." Genesis 38 tells how Judah failed to give his son to Tamar under the same custom. Naomi's point is bitter: she has no more sons, and even if she married and gave birth tonight, the boys would come too late. Chapter 4 will show a wider family form of this duty.

a: It is far more bitter for me than for you
t: More bitter than you, or bitter for your sake?
p: The Hebrew can be read two ways: "bitterer for me than for you" or "bitter for me because of you."
b: Hebrew mar li me'od mikkem is literally "bitter to me, very, from you." The little word min, "from," can mean "more than" or "because of." So Naomi says either "my lot is far more bitter than yours" (you are young and can remarry; I cannot) or, as in the KJV, "it grieves me much for your sakes." Both make sense. The Plain English Translation follows the first, held by many recent commentators, because Naomi goes on to explain that God's hand is against her in particular.

a: the hand of the LORD has gone out against me
p: Naomi blames God. Readers argue over whether the story agrees with her.
b: Naomi speaks like a lament psalm or like Job: God is behind her losses (compare Job 19:21; Psalm 88). Some ancient Jewish readers agreed, but put the blame on her family: the Targum says Elimelech and his sons were punished for leaving the land and marrying foreign women. Many modern readers think the book takes Naomi's complaint seriously without endorsing her conclusion, since the rest of the story shows God's quiet care through Ruth and Boaz. Others note that God is never shown correcting her, as he is not shown correcting Job's friends until the end (Job 42:7).

a: clung
p: Dabaq is the verb for a husband holding to his wife in Genesis 2:24.
b: The verb dabaq means to stick to or hold fast. A man "holds fast" to his wife (Genesis 2:24), and Israel is told to "hold fast" to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20; 30:20). Ruth makes that kind of commitment to her mother-in-law. The same verb returns in chapter 2, where Boaz tells Ruth to "stick close" to his young women (2:8, 21, 23), so her loyalty to Naomi leads her into Boaz's field. Boaz also calls her "my daughter" (2:8), as Naomi does, a hint that he is much older (compare 3:10).

a: her gods
p: Elohim can be plural or singular. Moab's chief god was Chemosh.
b: Elohim is plural in form. With Israel's God it means "God"; with other nations it can mean "gods" or one god. Moab's national god was Chemosh (Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:7, 33), named twelve times on the Mesha Stele, a Moabite victory inscription from about 840 BC in which King Mesha boasts of defeating Israel (compare 2 Kings 3). So Naomi may mean "her god" (YLT) or "her gods" (KJV, BSB). Either way, going home to Moab means going back to Moab's religion, which is why Ruth answers with "your God is my God."

a: where you go, I will go
p: These words are often read at weddings, but Ruth said them to her mother-in-law.
b: Ruth 1:16–17 is one of the most loved promises in the Bible and a common wedding reading. It is a vow between two widows, a young Moabite and an older Israelite, not between bride and groom. That does not make the wedding use wrong, since it is a picture of loyal love, but it is worth knowing who is speaking. The verbs are simple and personal: go, stay the night, die, be buried. Ruth gives up her country, her family, her religion and even her burial place.

a: Your people are my people, and your God is my God
p: Jewish tradition treats these words as the model for becoming Jewish. Christians see faith joining a people.
b: In Jewish tradition Ruth is the model convert. The Talmud reads Naomi's warnings as the questions a rabbi asks a convert, and Ruth's replies as her acceptance of the commandments (Talmud, Yevamot 47b; compare Ruth Rabbah). The Hebrew has no verb ("your people, my people"), so it can be read "will be" or, as here, "are": a decision already made. Her words join people and God: she joins Israel and Israel's God at once. Christians have read her as an early picture of the nations coming to Israel's God (Isaiah 56:3–7) and of Gentiles being grafted in (Romans 11:17; Ephesians 2:12–13, 19). Scholars note that formal conversion came later.

a: Thus may the LORD do to me, and more besides
t: An oath in the LORD's name
p: A standard Israelite oath, spoken by a Moabite, using the name of Israel's God.
b: "Thus may the LORD do to me, and more" is a fixed oath formula. The speaker calls down a curse on himself if he breaks his word, perhaps with a gesture like cutting the throat (1 Samuel 3:17; 2 Samuel 3:9; 1 Kings 19:2). Ruth swears by YHWH, not by Chemosh. The last clause is debated: "if anything but death separates us" (most versions) or "for death alone shall part us" (close to the YLT). Either way, only death will end her loyalty, and she means to be buried in Naomi's land.
orig: כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה יְהוָה לִי וְכֹה יֹסִיף (koh ya'aseh YHWH li vekhoh yosif)

a: Call me Mara
p: Naomi means "pleasant"; Mara means "bitter." Israel once met bitter water at a place called Marah.
b: Naomi renames herself: from Na'omi, "pleasant, my sweetness," to Mara, "bitter." The same word gave its name to Marah, where Israel found bitter water after crossing the sea and God made it sweet (Exodus 15:23–25). Naomi has used "bitter" already (1:13), and she pairs it with God's names: the Almighty has made her bitter. No one in the story ever calls her Mara. By the end the women are again speaking to "Naomi" (4:14, 17).

a: the Almighty
p: An ancient name of God whose exact meaning is uncertain. Job uses it more than any other book.
b: Shaddai, often El Shaddai, is the name God used with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3). "The Almighty" comes from the usual Greek and Latin renderings (pantokratōr, especially in Job, and omnipotens); the Greek of Ruth itself says ho hikanos, "the Sufficient One." Its original meaning is debated: some link it to a word for mountain ("God of the mountain"), others to shadad, "destroy," and others to shad, "breast," since it often appears in blessings of children (Genesis 49:25). It appears 31 times in Job, where it is also the God who has made a sufferer's life bitter (Job 27:2).

a: Full I went out, and empty the LORD has brought me back
t: Full and empty, with Ruth beside her
p: Naomi left with a husband and two sons. But Ruth is standing there as she speaks.
b: "Full" and "empty" are a key pair. Naomi left with a husband and two sons, and she comes back with none. Yet she left in a famine and returns at harvest, and Ruth is standing beside her. Some see honest grief that cannot yet see the gift in front of it. Others, notably Danna Nolan Fewell and David Gunn, and Tod Linafelt, read a colder Naomi, who says no more to Ruth on the road (1:18) and never mentions her here. Most readers see some of both. The book answers the word "empty" twice: Boaz will not let Ruth go back "empty" (3:17), and Naomi will hold a grandson in her lap (4:16).

a: Ruth the Moabite
p: The narrator keeps calling her "the Moabite," even after she has joined Israel.
b: The book calls Ruth "the Moabite" five times (1:22; 2:2, 21; 4:5, 10), and others call her a "Moabite" or a "foreigner" (2:6, 10). The label never goes away, even in the legal scene at the gate. Readers see two points: Ruth does not stop being a Moabite when she joins Israel, and the book wants its readers to remember exactly who David's great-grandmother was.

a: a man of great worth
p: Gibbor chayil can mean a war hero, a rich man or a man of strong character. Ruth gets the same word in 3:11.
b: Gibbor chayil is used of warriors (Judges 6:12; 11:1), of wealthy landowners (2 Kings 15:20) and of capable, honorable men (1 Samuel 9:1). The KJV says "a mighty man of wealth"; the BSB "a prominent man of noble character." Boaz is clearly well off and clearly good, so the Plain English Translation uses "worth" to hold both. The word matters because Boaz later calls Ruth an eshet chayil, "a woman of worth" (3:11), the same phrase as Proverbs 31:10. The man and the woman of worth are matched before they meet.

a: Boaz
p: Meaning uncertain, perhaps "in him is strength." A bronze pillar of Solomon's temple bore the name.
b: No one is sure what Boaz means. A common suggestion is "in him is strength" (bo + 'oz), but this is folk etymology, not proven. Solomon named the left-hand bronze pillar at the temple entrance Boaz and the right-hand one Jakin (1 Kings 7:21; 2 Chronicles 3:17). Why is not known; some think the name honored David's ancestor, but the Bible does not say so. Matthew and Luke list Boaz among Jesus' ancestors (Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32).

a: glean
p: Farmers had to leave the edges and leftovers of the harvest for the poor, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow.
b: Israel's law told farmers not to harvest the corners of their fields or go back for what they missed. The leftovers were "for the poor and for the foreigner" (Leviticus 19:9–10; 23:22) and to "the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" (Deuteronomy 24:19–22). Ruth is all three: poor, foreign and widowed. Gleaning was hard, hot work, and it depended on the landowner's goodwill, which is why Ruth hopes to find someone "in whose eyes I may find favor." The law gave her the right; Boaz will give her far more than the law asked.

a: As chance would have it, she happened to come
p: The Hebrew piles up the word "chance." The storyteller is winking: this is no accident.
b: Literally, "and her chance chanced upon" the part of the field that belonged to Boaz. The KJV has "her hap was to light on." The doubled word is so heavy that most readers take it as irony: from Ruth's side it was luck, but the reader is meant to see God's hand behind it. The "chances" in this book keep landing in the right place. Compare Joseph's words, "God planned it for good" (Genesis 50:20), and the hidden God of the book of Esther.

a: The LORD be with you!
p: A harvest-field greeting that became part of Christian worship.
b: Boaz greets his workers with a blessing, and they answer with one. The same words are said to Gideon (Judges 6:12) and, in Greek, to Mary (Luke 1:28). Christian worship has long used the exchange "The Lord be with you," "And also with you" (in Latin, Dominus vobiscum), and Ruth 2:4 is often cited as one of its roots. The greeting also tells us about Boaz: before we hear anything else, he speaks of the LORD to his laborers.

a: Let me glean, please, and gather among the sheaves
p: Gleaning among the cut bundles was more than the law allowed. Ruth may have been waiting for the owner's permission.
b: Gleaners normally picked up stray stalks after the bundles (sheaves) were gathered. Asking to glean "among the sheaves" was asking for more than usual, which is why Boaz later has to give that permission himself (2:15). Some scholars (Bush; Sasson) read the foreman's report this way: Ruth made a bold request, and the foreman told her to wait for the owner. That would explain why she "stood" from morning until Boaz arrived. Others read it as an ordinary gleaner's request, with the foreman praising her hard work. The verse is one of the hardest in the book. Its last clause is treated under "Manuscript differences."

a: I have ordered the young men not to touch you
t: A foreign woman alone in the fields
p: Boaz's order shows that a gleaner could be harassed or attacked. Naomi says the same in 2:22.
b: The verb "touch" (naga') can mean to harm, and with a woman it can mean sexual assault (Genesis 20:6; Genesis 26:11; Proverbs 6:29). A poor foreign widow working among male harvesters had no one to protect her. Boaz's first concern is her safety, and Naomi echoes it at the end of the chapter (2:22). In a book set in the days of Judges 19, this matters.

a: drink from what the young men have drawn
p: In Genesis women draw water for strangers. Here Israelite men draw water for a foreign woman.
b: Robert Alter has shown that Hebrew stories often meet future spouses at wells: Abraham's servant and Rebekah (Genesis 24), Jacob and Rachel (Genesis 29), Moses and Zipporah (Exodus 2:15–21). He calls this a "betrothal type-scene," a familiar pattern that storytellers vary on purpose. Ruth 2 plays with it: the foreigner is the woman, the setting is a field, and the men draw the water for her. A reader who knows the pattern can guess where this meeting is heading.

a: for you to notice me? I am a foreigner.
p: A play on words: lehakkireni, "to notice me," sounds like nokhriyyah, "a foreigner."
b: "Notice" (hikkir) and "foreigner" (nokhri) come from the same Hebrew root, nkr, which can mean both "recognize" and "be strange." Ruth asks, in effect, "Why do you know me, when I am an unknown?" English cannot keep the pun. Nokhriyyah is the word used for the foreign wives in Ezra 10:2 and Nehemiah 13:26–27, which matters for readers who think the book answers Ezra and Nehemiah.

a: You left your father and your mother and the land where you were born
p: Ruth did what God told Abraham to do: leave your land and your relatives and go.
b: God told Abram, "Go on your way, out of your land, away from your kin and from your father's house" (Genesis 12:1). Boaz describes Ruth in nearly the same terms, but Ruth had no promise from God when she left. The rabbis and many Christian readers have drawn the comparison: Abraham left his country to begin Israel, and Ruth left hers to join it. The phrase also echoes Genesis 2:24, where a man "leaves his father and his mother" and "sticks close" to his wife, with the Hebrew verb of 1:14, where Ruth clung to Naomi.

a: under whose wings you have come for refuge
p: A picture of a bird sheltering its young. Ruth will ask Boaz to spread his "wing" over her (3:9).
b: The psalms often picture God as a bird spreading its wings over its young: "Hide me in the shadow of your wings" (Psalm 17:8; see also Psalm 36:7; 57:1; 91:4). Jesus used the same image of himself and Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37). The word for wing, kanaf, also means the corner of a cloak. In 3:9 Ruth asks Boaz to spread his kanaf over her. Boaz prays that God will shelter her, and then he becomes the answer to his own prayer.

a: your servant girl
p: Here Ruth is a shifchah, the lowest servant. In 3:9 she is an amah, a servant who could be a wife.
b: Hebrew has two common words for a female servant. A shifchah is a low-ranking servant or slave. An amah is a servant who could also be a wife or concubine, someone inside the household (Genesis 30:3; 1 Samuel 25:41). Here Ruth uses shifchah and says she is not even equal to one of his shifchot. At the threshing floor she calls herself his amah (3:9). Many commentators see the change as a sign of her new boldness: she now speaks as a possible wife.

a: dip your piece in the vinegar
p: Bread dipped in sour wine and a handful of roasted grain: a field worker's meal, and Boaz serves it himself.
b: The "vinegar" (chomets) was a sour wine or wine vinegar, used as a dip and a refreshing drink for workers; it is related to the sour wine offered to Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:48). "Roasted grain" was fresh grain toasted over a fire (Leviticus 23:14; 1 Samuel 17:17). What stands out is that Boaz invites a foreign gleaner to sit with his own workers and serves her himself, giving her so much that she has leftovers to take home (2:18).

a: about an ephah of barley
p: Perhaps 30 pounds of grain from one day's gleaning. Common estimates put it at weeks of food.
b: An ephah was a dry measure, about two-thirds of a bushel by common modern estimates, though its exact size is uncertain and may have changed over time. Of barley it might weigh roughly 30 pounds (Hubbard; Block). Commentators often note that this was enough for two women for a few weeks, far more than one gleaner normally gathered in a day. The size of the haul is what makes Naomi ask at once, "Where did you glean today?" (2:19).

a: who has not abandoned his faithful love for the living and the dead
t: Whose faithful love: God's or Boaz's?
p: The Hebrew "who" could point back to the LORD or to Boaz. Both readings have strong support.
b: Hebrew asher, "who," could refer to the LORD (the nearest word) or to Boaz (the "he" being blessed). If it is the LORD, Naomi has stopped blaming God (1:13, 20–21) and now praises his loyalty to her and her dead husband and sons. If it is Boaz, she praises his kindness, as in Genesis 24:27, where similar wording refers to God. Many commentators think the ambiguity is the point: God's faithful love is reaching Naomi through Boaz. The Plain English Translation keeps the ambiguity as far as English allows.

a: one of our family redeemers
p: The go'el was the relative who rescued family: buying back land, freeing a slave, avenging a death.
b: The go'el was the near relative responsible for rescuing a family member in trouble. He bought back land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25), bought back a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49), and avenged a murder (Numbers 35:19). "Kinsman-redeemer" (many versions) and "next kinsman" (KJV) are attempts to say this. God calls himself Israel's go'el (Isaiah 41:14; 43:14), and Job cries, "I know that my redeemer lives" (Job 19:25). The word appears more than 20 times in Ruth. Naomi says Boaz is "one of" the redeemers, which prepares for 3:12.

a: Stick close to the young men who work for me
p: Boaz said "my young women" (2:8). Ruth says "my young men," and Naomi quietly corrects her.
b: In 2:8 Boaz told Ruth to stay close to his young women. Ruth reports it as his young men, using the masculine plural ne'arim, which can sometimes mean "workers" of both sexes. Naomi answers that it is good to go out "with his young women" (2:22). Readers take this as a touch of realism: an innocent slip, a general word for workers, a bit of humor, or a sign that Ruth is less worried than Naomi about the men in the field.

a: until the end of the barley harvest and the wheat harvest
p: Ruth arrived at the start of barley harvest and gleaned to the end of wheat harvest, about seven weeks.
b: Barley ripened first, around April, near Passover; the firstfruits of barley were offered at the start of harvest (Leviticus 23:10–14). Wheat harvest ended around the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot, later called Pentecost), counted as seven weeks from the first sheaf (Leviticus 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:9). Ruth arrived "at the beginning of the barley harvest" (1:22) and gleaned to the end of the wheat harvest, about two months, and in all that time nothing happened between her and Boaz. That pause is what pushes Naomi to act in chapter 3. Because the story fills this season, Jews read Ruth at Shavuot.

a: winnowing barley at the threshing floor
p: A flat, open place where grain was tossed into the evening breeze. Men often slept there to guard the harvest.
b: A threshing floor was a hard, flat area of rock or packed earth, often on a rise outside town. Grain was beaten or trampled to loosen it, then tossed into the air with a fork so the wind carried off the chaff, usually in the late afternoon and evening breeze. Owners slept there to guard the grain. Threshing floors also had a mixed reputation: Hosea condemns Israel for loving "the pay of a prostitute on every threshing floor" (Hosea 9:1). They could also be holy places: David bought the threshing floor of Araunah, and the temple was built there (2 Samuel 24:18–25; 2 Chronicles 3:1).

a: So bathe, rub on scented oil, put your cloak on
t: Dressed as a bride, or out of mourning?
p: Washing, oiling and changing clothes could mean the end of mourning, or getting ready for a wedding.
b: Washing, anointing with oil and changing clothes are what David did when he stopped mourning (2 Samuel 12:20), and what the woman of Tekoa was told not to do in order to look like a mourner (2 Samuel 14:2). They are also what God does for his bride in Ezekiel 16:9–12. So many readers see a widow signaling that her mourning is over and she is free to marry; others see a woman preparing like a bride; many see both. Jewish tradition also read the steps as a picture of conversion: Rashi, following earlier rabbis, explains "wash" as washing away idolatry and the clothes as Sabbath clothes. The "cloak" may simply be an outer garment for the night air.

a: uncover his feet
p: Margelot means the place of the feet or the legs. Readers have long debated how much the words imply.
b: Margelot is a rare word, from regel, "foot." It means the area at the feet or perhaps the legs (Daniel 10:6 uses it of legs). "Feet" can be a polite word for the private parts in Hebrew (Isaiah 7:20; perhaps Exodus 4:25), and "lie down" and "uncover" can have sexual meanings too, so some scholars read the scene as more daring than most translations suggest. Most commentators think the narrator uses double-edged words on purpose to build tension, but describes a proposal, not sex: Ruth uncovers the area at his feet and lies there until he wakes.

a: he was in a good mood
p: "His heart was good" means he was content after a good meal. It does not say he was drunk.
b: The Hebrew says "his heart was good." The phrase is used of people relaxed and happy after eating and drinking (Judges 19:6, 9; 1 Kings 21:7). It can go with too much wine (1 Samuel 25:36; Esther 1:10), but by itself it does not mean drunk. Some readers have pictured Boaz drunk, like Lot in Genesis 19:33, whose daughters became the mothers of Moab and Ammon. The parallel is real, and some think it is intended, but the contrast is the point: Boaz wakes, speaks clearly, and acts with honor.

a: Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant
p: A marriage request. Kanaf is the "wing" of 2:12 and the corner of a garment. God uses the same words in Ezekiel 16:8.
b: Kanaf means a wing or the corner, hem or edge of a cloak. To spread one's kanaf over a woman meant to take her as a wife. God says to Jerusalem, "I spread the wing of my cloak over you ... You were mine" (Ezekiel 16:8), and a law forbids a man to "uncover his father's kanaf," meaning his father's wife (Deuteronomy 22:30). Ruth's words also pick up Boaz's blessing: he prayed she would find refuge under the LORD's wings (2:12); now she asks him to spread his wing over her. The Plain English Translation adds "of your cloak" so the request is clear while keeping the image.

a: because you are a family redeemer
p: Marrying a widow and buying back land were separate customs. Ruth asks Boaz to do both.
b: The law nowhere says that the redeemer (go'el) must marry a widow; that was the brother-in-law's duty (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). Ruth links the two, asking Boaz as redeemer to marry her. Many scholars think this was Ruth's own creative appeal, going beyond Naomi's plan, which said only that Boaz would tell Ruth what to do (3:4). Others think local custom already joined the two duties, and that chapter 4 shows the law being applied that way. Either way, Ruth tells Boaz what to do, not the other way round.

a: This last act of faithful love is even greater than the first
p: The first was her loyalty to Naomi. The second is choosing a husband who can carry on her dead husband's family.
b: Most commentators take the "first" hesed to be Ruth's care for Naomi (2:11). The "last" is her coming to Boaz: instead of seeking a young husband of her own choice, rich or poor, she has sought a marriage inside Elimelech's family that can keep its name and land alive (4:10). Boaz's "my daughter" suggests a real age gap, which makes the choice more striking. So Ruth, the foreigner, is the person in the book most praised for hesed, the quality God claims for himself.
orig: הֵיטַבְתְּ חַסְדֵּךְ הָאַחֲרוֹן מִן־הָרִאשׁוֹן (heitavt chasdekh ha'acharon min-harishon)

a: the whole town knows
p: Literally "all the gate of my people," the town's public life. The scene at the gate in chapter 4 is coming.
b: The Hebrew says "all the gate of my people knows." The town gate was where people met, traded and held court, so "the gate" stands for the whole community, especially its men and leaders (compare Proverbs 31:23, 31). Boaz chooses the word just before he goes to that very gate (4:1). The KJV renders it "all the city of my people."

a: a woman of worth
t: Eshet chayil: the woman of Proverbs 31
p: The only woman in the Bible called this by name. In the Hebrew order, Ruth comes right after Proverbs 31.
b: Eshet chayil (KJV "a virtuous woman") is the phrase of Proverbs 31:10, "A woman of strength, who can find one?" and Proverbs 12:4. Ruth is the only named woman to receive it, and it matches the description of Boaz in 2:1. In many Hebrew Bibles Ruth follows Proverbs directly, so the reader goes from the poem about the woman of worth to a story about one. Many Jewish homes sing Proverbs 31 on Friday evenings, and Ruth is often remembered then.

a: there is a redeemer nearer than I am
p: Redemption went in order of kinship: brothers first, then uncles and cousins, then other relatives.
b: Leviticus 25:48–49 lists who may redeem a relative: a brother, an uncle, an uncle's son, or another close relative of the clan. The closer relative had the first right and duty. Jewish tradition (Ruth Rabbah; the Talmud, Bava Batra 91a) made Boaz the nephew of Elimelech and "So-and-so" his brother, but that is a later guess; the book does not say how either man was related. Boaz will not take a right that belongs to someone else, even at night with no witnesses.

a: It must not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor
t: What happened at the threshing floor?
p: Ancient and modern readers have argued about this night. Most conclude that nothing improper took place.
b: The rabbis praised Boaz's self-control. Ruth Rabbah compares him to Joseph, who refused Potiphar's wife (Genesis 39), and says he fought his desire all night. Christian commentators from the church fathers on have mostly agreed. No major commentary argues outright that the two had sex, though Danna Nolan Fewell and David Gunn leave the question open and read the scene suggestively. Most commentators argue that the story's whole shape, with Boaz's blessing, his insistence on the nearer redeemer and the public wedding, makes that unlikely. Boaz's concern for secrecy protects her reputation and his plan, not a guilty act.

a: six measures of barley
p: The Hebrew says only "six barleys." The unit is unknown. It was as much as she could carry.
b: The text says "six of barley" with no unit. Six ephahs (as in 2:17) would be far too heavy. The Targum says six seahs, but a seah is a third of an ephah, so that would be two ephahs, twice Ruth's whole day's gleaning; the Targum knows this and adds that God gave her strength to carry it. Many modern readers think of six scoops or handfuls, and the KJV supplies "measures." The Targum and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 93a–b) also saw a sign in the number: six blessed descendants would come from Ruth, and both lists include David and the Messiah. The plain point is generosity, and a message to Naomi that Ruth does not come back empty (3:17).

a: Who are you, my daughter?
p: Naomi asks the same words Boaz asked at midnight. It probably means "How did it go?"
b: Boaz asked "Who are you?" in the dark (3:9). Naomi asks the same Hebrew question at dawn, with "my daughter" added. She knows who Ruth is, so most versions translate the sense: "How did it go?" (BSB) or "How did you fare?" But the literal words may also mean "Who are you now?": still the widow of Mahlon, or the promised wife of Boaz? The Plain English Translation keeps the words so the echo can be heard.

a: Do not come to your mother-in-law empty
p: The word "empty" from Naomi's complaint in 1:21 comes back. These words appear only in Ruth's report.
b: In 1:21 Naomi said the LORD had brought her back "empty" (reqam). Here Ruth reports that Boaz said she must not go to her mother-in-law "empty." Interestingly, the narrator did not include these words when telling the scene (3:15); they appear only here, in Ruth's report to Naomi. Either way, the gift answers Naomi's complaint directly. The emptiness of chapter 1 is being filled, first with grain and soon with a child.

a: Boaz went up to the town gate and sat down there
p: The gate was the town's courthouse and town hall. Excavated Iron Age gates have stone benches in or beside them.
b: Israelite towns had a fortified gate with rooms on each side, and the open space there served as market, meeting place and court. Elders sat there to judge cases and witness agreements (Deuteronomy 21:19; 22:15; 25:7; Amos 5:15). Excavated Iron Age gates have stone benches in or beside them: at Dan a long bench stands against the gate complex, and at Gezer benches line the gate chambers. Everyone going out to the fields in the morning had to pass through, so Boaz could be sure the nearer redeemer would come by.

a: So-and-so
p: The Hebrew peloni almoni is like "so-and-so." The narrator will not tell us the man's name.
b: Peloni almoni means something like "Mr. So-and-so" or "such and such a one," a rhyming phrase for a person or place left unnamed (1 Samuel 21:2; 2 Kings 6:8). Boaz surely used the man's name; the narrator chose to hide it. Many readers see a lesson: the man who would not keep a dead man's name alive (4:6) loses his own name in the story, while Boaz's name is still known.

a: ten men from the elders of the town
p: Ten elders as witnesses. The Talmud used this verse for the rule of ten men at wedding blessings.
b: The law does not fix a number of elders for such a case, but ten is a round, complete number. Later Jewish law requires a quorum (minyan) of ten adult men for public prayer and for the seven wedding blessings, and the Talmud (Ketubot 7b) cites this verse as a source for the wedding rule. Here the ten make the agreement public and binding, so no one can later question Ruth's marriage or Obed's inheritance.

a: is selling it
p: The verb form could mean Naomi "has sold" the land or "is selling" it. And how did a widow own land?
b: Hebrew makherah is in a form that usually means a finished action, "has sold" (KJV "selleth"), but it can also mean an action announced as done right now, "is hereby selling." Scholars also debate how Naomi could have land to sell, since inheritance law usually passed land to sons (Numbers 27:8–11). Suggestions include: she held the use of it as a widow; it had been sold or pledged when the family left, and she now sold her right to redeem it; or local custom allowed widows to hold land. The book does not explain, perhaps because its first readers knew.

a: uncover your ear
p: An idiom for "tell you." It uses the verb galah, the same verb as "uncover his feet" in chapter 3.
b: "Uncover the ear" means to let someone know something (1 Samuel 20:2; 2 Samuel 7:27). The verb is galah, the same one Naomi and the narrator used for Ruth uncovering Boaz's feet (3:4, 7), a verb that can also carry a sexual sense. Many commentators think the echo is deliberate: what was uncovered secretly at night is now uncovered publicly in the morning, at the gate.

a: in order to raise up the dead man's name on his inheritance
t: Why the redeemer changed his mind
p: Buying land was a good deal. Marrying Ruth meant the land would go to her son as Mahlon's heir.
b: The nearer redeemer was glad to buy Elimelech's land (4:4). But if he also married Ruth, her first son would count as Mahlon's heir and inherit that land, so the redeemer would spend money on property that would not stay in his own family, and might have to divide his own estate among more children (4:6). Most scholars explain the turn this way. They disagree on whether marrying Ruth was a legal duty that came with the land (a wider form of Deuteronomy 25:5–10), or a moral claim that Boaz cleverly attached to it. The phrase "raise up the dead man's name" comes straight from the brother-in-law law.

a: or I will damage my own inheritance
p: He would pay for land that would later belong to Ruth's son, not to his own children.
b: The man does not refuse out of malice. His reason is economic and family-minded: he would pay the price of the field, then support Ruth and her child, and in the end the field would pass to that child as Mahlon's heir. His own children's share would shrink. The Targum adds that he already had a wife and feared strife at home, but the text says only that he would "ruin" or "damage" (shachat) his inheritance. He acts legally and sensibly, and that is the contrast: Boaz and Ruth both act with hesed, beyond what sense and law require.

a: in earlier times
p: The narrator stops to explain an old custom, which shows the book was written some time after the events.
b: "Now this was the custom in Israel in earlier times" is an aside to the reader, like 1 Samuel 9:9 ("the one now called a prophet was called a seer back then"). It shows that the writer lived long enough after the story that the sandal custom needed explaining. How long is debated: those who date the book to the time of David or Solomon think a few generations was enough; those who date it after the exile see a gap of many centuries. Either way, it is evidence that the book was written down well after the days of the judges.

a: a man pulled off his sandal and gave it to the other man
p: A sandal stood for the right to walk on and possess land. Here it is a sign of transfer, not shame.
b: In Deuteronomy 25:9–10 a widow pulls the sandal off a brother-in-law who refuses to marry her and spits in his face, a public shaming. Here there is no shame and no widow involved: the man hands over his own sandal to confirm a transfer of rights. Setting foot on land was a way of claiming it (Joshua 1:3), and "over Edom I throw my sandal" is a claim of ownership (Psalm 60:8). E. A. Speiser pointed to texts from ancient Nuzi in which shoes appear in property deals, though how close the parallel is remains debated. Who gave the sandal to whom is itself debated (see "Manuscript differences" at 4:8).

a: I am also acquiring Ruth the Moabite
p: The KJV says "purchased," but qanah means to acquire. Boaz bought land; he married Ruth.
b: The verb qanah is used for buying land (4:9) and for "acquiring" Ruth (4:10). The KJV's "purchased" can make it sound as if Ruth was sold. But qanah means to acquire or get in a broad sense: Eve "got" a son from the LORD (Genesis 4:1), and God "made" or "acquired" his people (Exodus 15:16). No price is paid for Ruth. Boaz's words are the legal announcement of a marriage, made before witnesses, in which he takes on duties to her, to Naomi and to Mahlon's name.

a: like Rachel and Leah, the two who built the house of Israel
p: The two wives of Jacob, mothers of Israel's tribes. Rachel was buried near Bethlehem.
b: Rachel and Leah, with their servants Bilhah and Zilpah, were the mothers of Jacob's twelve sons (Genesis 29:31–30:24; 35:23–26). "Build a house" is a Hebrew way of saying "have children," with a pun on banah, "build," and ben, "son." Rachel, the younger, is named first, perhaps because she was buried near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19–20), though Leah was the mother of Judah, Boaz's ancestor. A foreign woman is blessed to stand beside the mothers of Israel.

a: the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah
p: Tamar was another childless widow who took bold action to get a son from a man of Judah's family.
b: Genesis 38 tells how Judah's sons died and he failed to give his last son to Tamar, his widowed daughter-in-law. She disguised herself, became pregnant by Judah himself, and bore twins, Perez and Zerah. Judah admitted, "She is more in the right than I am" (Genesis 38:26). The parallels with Ruth are close: a widow with no child, a foreign or outsider woman, an older man of Judah, an unusual approach, and a son who carries on the family line. Perez was the ancestor of Bethlehem's clan (1 Chronicles 2:4–5, 9–15).

a: the LORD let her become pregnant
p: Only the second time the narrator says God acted. After ten childless years in Moab, Ruth conceives.
b: The narrator rarely says what God did. Characters bless and pray in God's name throughout, but the narrator's own voice credits God directly only twice: when the LORD "had come to help his people by giving them bread" (1:6), and here. Ruth had been married about ten years in Moab with no child (1:4), a grief and a danger in a world where children carried on a family's name and cared for parents in old age. The Hebrew wording, "the LORD gave her conception," is used nowhere else. The two acts of God bracket the story: food for the land, and a child for the family. Compare the long waits of Sarah, Rachel and Hannah.
orig: וַיִּתֵּן יְהוָה לָהּ הֵרָיוֹן (vayyitten YHWH lah herayon)

a: May his name be proclaimed in Israel
p: The child's name or the LORD's? The Hebrew could point to either.
b: The "his" could refer to the LORD, just blessed, or to the redeemer the LORD has provided. Most translators take it as the child: the women pray that the boy will be famous, and the next verses are about him. Some take it as the LORD, whose name the child's birth makes known. The "redeemer" here is the newborn, not Boaz, since the women go on to say what "he" will do for Naomi in her old age.

a: He will bring back your life
p: Meshiv nefesh, "one who brings back life," uses the "return" verb of chapter 1.
b: The women call the child meshiv nefesh, literally "one who brings back the soul (life)." The exact phrase is used of food or comfort that revives someone in Lamentations 1:11, 16, 19, and a close form describes God's law "reviving the soul" in Psalm 19:7. The verb is shuv, the "return" word of chapter 1, also used, in another form, in "he restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Naomi returned empty (1:21), and now a child will return her life to her.

a: worth more to you than seven sons
p: Seven sons was the picture of a perfect family. The women say Ruth is worth more.
b: In Israel, seven sons stood for complete blessing: Hannah sings that "The childless woman bears seven" (1 Samuel 2:5), and Job had seven sons (Job 1:2; 42:13). For the women of Bethlehem to say that a Moabite daughter-in-law is "better than seven sons" is extraordinary praise. It also answers 1:11–13, where Naomi grieved that she had no sons to offer. Here, too, the women speak of Ruth's love for Naomi.

a: became his nurse
t: Naomi's role: nurse or adoptive mother?
p: Omenet means a caregiver or guardian. Some scholars think Naomi formally adopted the child.
b: Omenet appears elsewhere only for Mephibosheth's nurse (2 Samuel 4:4). It is the feminine of omen, a guardian or foster parent, used of Moses carrying Israel "the way a foster father carries a nursing baby" (Numbers 11:12), of the guardians of Ahab's sons (2 Kings 10:1, 5), and of kings as Israel's foster fathers (Isaiah 49:23). It does not require breastfeeding. Some scholars, such as Gillis Gerleman and Ludwig Köhler, see a formal adoption rite in placing the child "in her lap" (compare Genesis 30:3; 48:12), but others find no clear evidence for such a rite in Israel. In any case, the women at once say, "A son is born to Naomi" (4:17).
r: 2 Samuel 4:4; Numbers 11:12; 2 Kings 10:1; Isaiah 49:23; Genesis 30:3; Genesis 48:12

a: The women who lived nearby gave him a name
p: The only child in the Bible named by the women of the neighborhood. Obed means "servant" or "worker."
b: Parents normally named their children in the Bible, usually the mother (Genesis 29:32–30:24; 1 Samuel 1:20) and sometimes the father. Only here do neighbors give the name. It shows how much the whole community has taken in Naomi and Ruth. Obed means "one who serves" or "worker," perhaps short for Obadiah, "servant of the LORD." The story ends by jumping ahead two generations: Obed is the grandfather of David. Everything in the book has been leading here.

a: the father of Jesse, the father of David
p: The last word of the story is "David." Later, David sent his parents to Moab for safety.
b: The book's last narrative word is "David." Ruth, the Moabite, is David's great-grandmother. When Saul hunted David, he took his father and mother to the king of Moab for safety (1 Samuel 22:3–4), which may reflect this family link. Jesse is introduced in 1 Samuel 16. The connection made Ruth important for both Jews and Christians: a foreigner is built into the family of Israel's greatest king, and, for Christians, of Jesus, the "son of David" (Matthew 1:1, 5).

a: these are the generations of Perez
p: "These are the generations" is the phrase that organizes Genesis. The list of ten names runs from Perez to David.
b: Elleh toledot, "these are the generations," organizes the book of Genesis (Genesis 2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 11:27; 25:19; 37:2). Ruth's list has ten names, Perez to David, like the ten from Adam to Noah (Genesis 5) and from Shem to Abram (Genesis 11:10–26). Boaz is seventh and David tenth, both places of honor in ancient lists, as Jack Sasson has pointed out. The same line appears in 1 Chronicles 2:5–15 and in Jesus' genealogies (Matthew 1:3–6; Luke 3:31–33). Many critical scholars think the list was added later; others think the book was written to end with it. The list also leaves gaps (see 4:21).
r: Genesis 2:4; Genesis 5:1; Genesis 11:10–26; 1 Chronicles 2:5–15; Matthew 1:3–6; Luke 3:31–33

a: Nahshon
p: Nahshon led the tribe of Judah in the wilderness under Moses. His sister married Aaron.
b: Nahshon son of Amminadab was the leader of Judah in the time of Moses (Numbers 1:7; 2:3), the first to bring an offering at the dedication of the altar (Numbers 7:12–17), and the brother of Elisheba, Aaron's wife (Exodus 6:23). A later Jewish tradition says he was the first to jump into the Red Sea before it parted. With Nahshon in the list, the line runs from the Exodus to the monarchy in a few names.

a: Salmon fathered Boaz
p: From the Exodus to David is two to four centuries, too long for five generations. Most think the list skips names.
b: Nahshon lived in Moses' day. David was born about 1040 BC, so the gap is about 220 years if the Exodus is dated about 1260 BC, and about 400 years if it is dated by 1 Kings 6:1 (about 1446 BC). Five generations from Nahshon to David would require each father to have the son in the list at a very old age. Most scholars, conservative and critical alike, think the list is selective, as ancient genealogies often were, naming important ancestors and skipping others. Matthew adds that Salmon's wife was Rahab (Matthew 1:5); if that is the Rahab of Jericho, it also suggests gaps.

a: Jesse fathered David
t: The four women in Matthew's list
p: Matthew adds four women to this line: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba.
b: Matthew 1:3–6 copies this line and adds four mothers: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and "the wife of Uriah," Bathsheba. All four were foreigners or linked to foreigners, and all four had stories that raised eyebrows. Interpreters suggest Matthew includes them to show that God works through outsiders and unexpected people, preparing for a Messiah for the nations (Matthew 28:19). Ruth is the only one of the four with a book of her own.
